# Strategy as a subject of study (`strategy_theory`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: helped by alphabet_writing, printing_press, game_theory
- Core idea: War is a tool of policy and not an end: the aim is a better peace, and force must be measured against that aim (Clausewitz). The best victory breaks the enemy's plan or alliances without battle; know the enemy and yourself; strike where he is unprepared (Sun Tzu). Real war is ruled by friction, chance and fear, so simple plans and reserves beat clever ones; the defence is the stronger form of war; every offensive weakens as it advances and has a culminating point. These ideas can be taught from recorded cases, and states that study past wars systematically make fewer of the old mistakes.
- Pitfalls:
  - Quoting Sun Tzu's maxims as recipes; they are reminders, and the opponent has read them too
  - Reading Clausewitz as a prophet of total war; his point is that politics limits and directs war
  - Confusing tactics (winning the fight) with strategy (using fights for the purpose of the war)
  - Planning on what the enemy will probably do instead of what he can do
- History: china: c. 5th–4th c. BC – Sunzi bingfa (author and date debated; text known from a tomb copy of c. 140–118 BC); 1080 – Seven Military Classics made the examination canon; india: c. 1st c. BC – 3rd c. AD – Arthashastra, books 9–13 on campaigns (traditionally ascribed to Kautilya, c. 300 BC); greece: c. 400 BC – Thucydides analyses strategy and policy; c. 350 BC – Aeneas Tacticus, the oldest surviving Greek military manual; rome: c. AD 84–96 – Frontinus, Stratagems; c. AD 400 – Vegetius, the most read military book of medieval and Renaissance Europe; islamic: 14th c. – Mamluk furusiyya manuals; europe: c. 600 – Byzantine Strategikon attributed to Maurice; 1521 – Machiavelli, Arte della guerra; 1832 – Clausewitz, Vom Kriege; 1838 – Jomini; 1890 – Mahan on sea power
- Read:
  - Sun Tzu, The Art of War (tr. Samuel B. Griffith, 1963)
  - Carl von Clausewitz, On War (1832; tr. Michael Howard & Peter Paret, 1976)
  - Lawrence Freedman, Strategy: A History (2013)
